learn: Fast facts come from strategies you can use in your head.
Doubles (7 + 7 = 14) and near doubles (7 + 8 = 15) are quick.
Making ten is another: 9 + 6 is 10 + 5 = 15.
lessons.try: Solve 8 + 7 two different ways.

learn: Think addition to subtract: 15 - 9 means 9 + ? = 15. The answer is 6.
Count up from the smaller number: from 9 to 15 is 6.
Subtracting from 10 is easy if you know your tens facts: 10 - 3 = 7.
lessons.try: Solve 16 - 8 by thinking addition.

learn: A fact family shows how three numbers work together: 6 + 7 = 13, 7 + 6 = 13, 13 - 6 = 7, 13 - 7 = 6.
Practise facts a little every day to make them automatic.
When facts are fast, harder problems are easier.
check: Which is in the fact family 6, 7, 13?
lessons.try: Write the fact family for 5, 9 and 14.

learn: A double adds a number to itself: 4 + 4 = 8, 7 + 7 = 14.
Doubles are easy to remember. Think of legs on animals or eggs in a carton.
Knowing doubles helps with many other facts.
lessons.try: Say all the doubles from 1 + 1 to 10 + 10.

learn: A near double is one more than a double: 6 + 7 is 6 + 6 + 1.
Look for numbers that are next to each other.
lessons.try: Solve 5 + 6, 8 + 9 and 7 + 8 using doubles.

learn: Make a ten to add quickly: 9 + 5 = 9 + 1 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14.
Break the smaller number to fill the ten.
A ten frame shows this clearly.
check: To make ten with 7, you need...
lessons.try: Use a ten frame to solve 8 + 6.

learn: Start with the bigger number and count on the smaller one.
8 + 3: start at 8, count 9, 10, 11.
Counting on is good for adding 1, 2 or 3.
check: Start counting on from the ___ number.
lessons.try: Count on to solve five facts.

learn: To solve 13 − 5, think: 5 + ? = 13.
Addition facts help with subtraction.
lessons.try: Solve 14 − 6 by thinking addition.

learn: Counting back takes away by counting down.
12 − 3: start at 12, count back 11, 10, 9.
Counting back works best for subtracting 1, 2 or 3.
check: Counting back is best for subtracting small...
lessons.try: Count back on a number line.

learn: For 15 − 7, take 5 to get to 10, then 2 more to get 8.
Going back through ten makes it easier.
lessons.try: Solve 16 − 8 by going back to ten.

learn: A fact family uses three numbers to make four facts.
Knowing one fact gives you three more.
lessons.try: Write the fact family for 6, 7, 13.

learn: Sometimes one number is missing: 7 + ? = 15.
Think: what plus 7 makes 15? It's 8.
Use fact families to find missing numbers.
lessons.try: Solve five missing-number puzzles.

learn: Read the problem, find the numbers and decide: join or take away?
"Ana has 9 shells. She finds 6 more." That's join: 9 + 6 = 15.
Always write the answer with a label.
check: Ana has 9 shells and finds 6 more. How many?
There are 14 birds. 5 fly away. How many are left?
lessons.try: Solve and draw three word problems.

learn: Games help you learn facts fast.
Play flash cards, dice games and fact races with a partner.
Practise a little every day.
lessons.try: Play "roll and add" with two dice for five minutes.

learn: You now have many strategies: doubles, make ten, count on, think addition.
Pick the fastest one for each fact.
Fast facts make bigger maths easier.
lessons.try: Take a two-minute facts check and track your score.

learn: An even number of objects can be put into pairs with none left over.
An odd number always has one left over.
6 socks make 3 pairs: even. 7 socks make 3 pairs and 1 extra: odd.
lessons.try: Pair up a pile of buttons. Is the number odd or even?

learn: You can tell if a number is even by looking at its ones digit.
If it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8, it is even.
If it ends in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9, it is odd.
check: Which digit makes a number odd?
lessons.try: Decide if 34, 57, 80 and 91 are odd or even.

learn: An even number can be written as a doubles fact: 12 = 6 + 6.
An odd number cannot be split into two equal whole numbers: 11 = 5 + 6.
This is another way to check odd and even.
check: Can 11 be split into two equal whole numbers?
lessons.try: Write 10, 14 and 18 as doubles.

learn: Put objects into pairs, two by two.
If every object has a partner, the number is even.
If one is left over, the number is odd.
check: A number with no leftover is...
lessons.try: Pair up counters for 7, 8 and 10.

learn: Even numbers are 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and so on.
They can be shared equally between two people.
Even numbers count by twos from zero.
check: Even numbers can be shared equally between...
lessons.try: Count by twos to 30.

learn: Odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and so on.
When you share them between two, one is left over.
Odd and even numbers take turns on a number line.
check: Sharing an odd number between two leaves ___ over.
lessons.try: Colour odd numbers on a hundred chart.

learn: Look at the ones digit to tell odd or even.
Ending in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 is even. Ending in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 is odd.
346 ends in 6, so it's even.
check: To tell odd or even, look at the ___ digit.
lessons.try: Sort ten three-digit numbers into odd and even.

learn: Every even number is a double: 10 = 5 + 5, 14 = 7 + 7.
Odd numbers can't be split into two equal whole numbers.
Writing a double proves a number is even.
check: Can 11 be split into two equal whole numbers?
lessons.try: Write each even number to 20 as a double.

learn: Even + even = even. Odd + odd = even.
Even + odd = odd.
lessons.try: Test the rules with five sums.

learn: An array is objects in equal rows and columns.
3 rows of 4 is 12 objects.
Arrays help us count quickly.
lessons.try: Build an array of 3 rows of 5 with counters.

learn: Arrays can be added row by row: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
This is called repeated addition.
It leads to multiplication later.
check: Repeated addition adds the ___ number again and again.
lessons.try: Write a repeated addition sentence for an egg carton.

learn: Arrays can be up to 5 rows and 5 columns.
5 rows of 5 makes 25.
Count by rows or by columns.
lessons.try: Draw a 4 by 5 array and count it two ways.

lessons.t: Odd and Even in Real Life
learn: House numbers are often odd on one side of the street and even on the other.
Pairs of socks and shoes come in twos.
Teams of two need an even number of players.
check: 12 players can make teams of two with...
If one side of the street is odd, the other is often...
lessons.try: Look at house numbers on the class map and sort them.

learn: Use the rules to solve puzzles.
"I'm even, between 10 and 15, and a double of 6." Answer: 12.
Check each clue.
check: I'm odd, between 6 and 8. I am...
I'm even and a double of 9. I am...
I'm odd, between 20 and 22. I am...
lessons.try: Make your own odd/even riddle.

learn: Even numbers pair up. Odd numbers have one left over.
The ones digit tells you which.
Arrays and repeated addition show equal groups.
lessons.try: Play odd-even dice: roll and say odd or even fast.

learn: Ten tens make one hundred.
A three-digit number has hundreds, tens and ones. In 352, there are 3 hundreds, 5 tens and 2 ones.
352 = 300 + 50 + 2. This is expanded form.
lessons.try: Show 246 with drawings of hundreds squares, tens sticks and ones dots.

learn: 407 is read "four hundred seven". The zero holds the tens place.
Numbers can be written as digits, words or expanded form.
1,000 is ten hundreds.
check: How do you write "four hundred seven"?
What does the zero in 407 do?
lessons.try: Write 619 in words and in expanded form.

learn: Compare hundreds first, then tens, then ones.
523 > 489 because 5 hundreds is more than 4 hundreds.
361 < 367 because the hundreds and tens match, and 1 one is less than 7 ones.
lessons.try: Compare 708 and 780. Which is greater?

learn: Ten ones make a ten. Ten tens make a hundred.
Bundle straws in tens to count big piles fast.
10 bundles of ten = 100.
lessons.try: Bundle 134 straws into hundreds, tens and ones.

learn: Flats show hundreds, rods show tens and cubes show ones.
2 flats, 3 rods and 5 cubes = 235.
Blocks help you see a number's size.
lessons.try: Build 312 with base-ten blocks.

learn: The place of a digit tells its value.
In 472, the 4 means 400, the 7 means 70 and the 2 means 2.
The same digit can be worth different amounts.
lessons.try: Tell the value of each digit in 658.

learn: Expanded form shows each place's value: 527 = 500 + 20 + 7.
It breaks a number into parts.
Zero places are left out: 405 = 400 + 5.
lessons.try: Write five numbers in expanded form.

learn: Write numbers in words: 243 is two hundred forty-three.
Use a hyphen in numbers like forty-three.
Don't say "and" in whole numbers.
lessons.try: Write the number name for 615 and 870.

learn: Zero holds a place when there are none of something.
507 has 5 hundreds, 0 tens and 7 ones.
Without zero, 507 would look like 57.
lessons.try: Build 507 and 570 with blocks and compare.

learn: Count by ones, tens and hundreds to 1,000.
After 199 comes 200. After 999 comes 1,000.
1,000 is ten hundreds.
lessons.try: Count by hundreds to 1,000.

learn: Ten more changes the tens digit up by one: 346 → 356.
Ten less changes it down by one: 346 → 336.
The ones digit stays the same.
lessons.try: Find 10 more and 10 less than five numbers.

learn: 100 more changes the hundreds digit up by one: 346 → 446.
100 less changes it down by one: 346 → 246.
The tens and ones stay the same.
lessons.try: Play a 100 more, 100 less card game.

learn: Use > for greater than, < for less than and = for equal.
Compare hundreds first, then tens, then ones.
463 > 436 because 6 tens is more than 3 tens.
lessons.try: Compare six pairs of numbers.

learn: Put numbers in order from least to greatest.
Compare the hundreds first.
128, 182, 218, 281 are in order from least.
lessons.try: Order five three-digit numbers.

learn: Hundreds, tens and ones tell a number's size.
Expanded form, number names and symbols show numbers different ways.
Ten of any place makes one of the next.
lessons.try: Play "build my number" with a partner.

learn: Skip counting means counting by a number other than one.
Skip counting helps count money and tell time.
check: Six nickels is how many cents?
lessons.try: Count nickels by fives.

learn: Counting by hundreds: 100, 200, 300, up to 1,000.
You can start from other numbers: 150, 250, 350.
Only the hundreds digit changes.
check: When you count by hundreds, which digit changes?
lessons.try: Count by hundreds from 120 to 920.

learn: Skip counting makes equal jumps on a number line.
Starting at 0 with jumps of 5 lands on 5, 10, 15.
Finding the missing number: 35, 40, ?, 50. The jump is 5, so the answer is 45.
check: Skip counting makes jumps that are...
lessons.try: Draw a number line with jumps of 10 from 0 to 100.

learn: Skip counting by twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10...
It's faster than counting by ones.
Use it for pairs of things.
check: Counting by twos is good for...
lessons.try: Count pairs of shoes in the class by twos.

lessons.t: Counting by Fives From Any Number
learn: Skip count by fives: 5, 10, 15, 20...
You can start from other numbers: 3, 8, 13, 18.
The ones digit takes turns in a pattern.
lessons.try: Count by fives from 7 to 52.

lessons.t: Counting by Tens From Any Number
learn: Count by tens: 10, 20, 30...
From 4: 4, 14, 24, 34. The ones stay the same.
Only the tens digit changes.
check: Counting by tens, the ___ digit stays the same.
lessons.try: Count by tens from 26 to 126.

learn: Count by hundreds: 100, 200, 300...
Only the hundreds digit changes.
lessons.try: Count by hundreds from 75 to 975.

learn: Nickels count by fives. Dimes count by tens.
Three dimes is 10, 20, 30 cents.
Skip counting helps count money quickly.
lessons.try: Count a pile of dimes and nickels.

learn: You can skip count backward: 50, 45, 40, 35.
Backward by tens: 90, 80, 70.
This helps with subtraction.
lessons.try: Count back by tens from 200 to 100.

learn: On a hundred chart, counting by tens goes straight down.
Counting by fives makes two columns.
Charts help you see number patterns.
check: Counting by tens on a hundred chart goes...
Counting by fives lands in columns ending in...
Below 23 on a hundred chart is...
lessons.try: Colour all fives on a hundred chart.

learn: Show skip counting with jumps on a number line.
Each jump is the same size.
Count the jumps to find the total.
check: Four jumps of 5 from 0 lands on...
Jumps on a skip-count line are the ___ size.
Three jumps of 10 from 0 lands on...
lessons.try: Draw jumps of 5 from 0 to 40.

learn: A pattern rule tells how numbers change.
12, 15, 18, 21 has the rule "add 3".
Check the rule works for every step.
lessons.try: Find the rule for three number patterns.

learn: Use the rule to fill gaps: 25, 30, __, 40.
The rule is add 5, so the missing number is 35.
Check the numbers on both sides.
lessons.try: Fill in five patterns with gaps.

learn: Use skip counting in stories.
"A spider has 8 legs. How many legs on 3 spiders?" 8, 16, 24.
Skip count by the group size.
lessons.try: Solve and draw a skip-counting story.

learn: Skip count by 2s, 5s, 10s and 100s.
Start anywhere and go forwards or backwards.
Patterns have rules you can find.
lessons.try: Skip-count relay with your team.

learn: To add 34 + 25, add tens: 30 + 20 = 50. Add ones: 4 + 5 = 9. Total: 59.
Breaking numbers into tens and ones is called decomposing.
You can draw tens sticks and ones dots to show it.
check: Breaking numbers into tens and ones is called...
lessons.try: Add 42 + 36 by adding tens and ones.

learn: When the ones add to 10 or more, make a new ten. This is regrouping.
47 + 25: 7 + 5 = 12 ones, which is 1 ten and 2 ones. 40 + 20 + 10 = 70. Total: 72.
In written work, carry the new ten to the tens column.
check: When ones add to 10 or more, you...
lessons.try: Add 38 + 46 with regrouping.

learn: You can add up to four two-digit numbers.
Look for friendly numbers that make tens: 25 + 15 = 40.
Then add the rest: 40 + 33 = 73.
check: Which pair makes a friendly ten?

learn: Adding tens is like adding ones: 3 tens + 4 tens = 7 tens.
Only the tens digit changes.
lessons.try: Add tens with rods.

learn: The ones digit stays the same.
Count on by tens on a hundred chart.
lessons.try: Add 20 and 30 to five numbers.

learn: Jump to add on an open number line.
36 + 25: jump 20 to 56, then 5 to 61.
Big jumps of ten first, then small jumps.
lessons.try: Solve three sums on an open number line.

learn: Break both numbers into tens and ones.
Add tens, add ones, then put together.
lessons.try: Break apart and add 43 + 36.

learn: Sometimes the ones add to 10 or more.
27 + 15: 7 + 5 = 12. That's one more ten and 2 ones.
lessons.try: Use blocks to add 38 + 24.

learn: Line up tens and ones in columns.
Add ones first. If 10 or more, write the ones and carry 1 ten.
Then add the tens, including the carried one.
lessons.try: Solve 46 + 37 in columns.

learn: Make one number friendly: 39 + 25 = 40 + 25 − 1 = 64.
Change a number to the nearest ten, then fix it.
Great for numbers ending in 8 or 9.
lessons.try: Solve 29 + 46 and 58 + 17 by compensation.

learn: Look for pairs that make ten first.
Order doesn't change the sum.
check: Order of adding changes the sum?
lessons.try: Add three numbers looking for tens.

learn: Add up to four two-digit numbers.
Group friendly pairs, then add.
lessons.try: Add the scores of four players.

learn: Estimate first so you know if your answer is sensible.
If you get 179, something is wrong.
check: Estimating helps you check if an answer is...
lessons.try: Estimate, then solve three sums.

learn: Find the numbers and decide to add.
"There are 45 red apples and 38 green ones. How many apples?" 45 + 38 = 83.
Draw a bar model if it helps.
check: 45 red apples and 38 green apples make...
lessons.try: Solve three addition word problems.

learn: You can add with tens, number lines, breaking apart, columns and compensation.
Choose the strategy that's quickest for you.
Always check with an estimate.
lessons.try: Solve five sums using five different strategies.

learn: To subtract 68 - 25, subtract tens: 60 - 20 = 40. Subtract ones: 8 - 5 = 3. Answer: 43.
Always subtract the smaller ones from the larger ones when you can.
Check by adding: 43 + 25 = 68.
lessons.try: Solve 79 - 34 and check with addition.

learn: Sometimes there are not enough ones. Break a ten into ten ones.
52 - 17: you can't take 7 from 2. Trade a ten: 4 tens and 12 ones. 12 - 7 = 5. 40 - 10 = 30. Answer: 35.
This is regrouping, sometimes called borrowing.
check: When there aren't enough ones, you...
lessons.try: Solve 63 - 28 with regrouping.

learn: Some problems need two steps.
"Mia had 45 stickers. She got 20 more, then gave 15 away. How many now?" 45 + 20 = 65. 65 - 15 = 50.
Read carefully, plan each step and check your answer makes sense.
check: Mia had 45, got 20, gave 15 away. How many now?
lessons.try: Make up a two-step story problem for a friend.

learn: Subtract tens like ones: 8 tens − 3 tens = 5 tens.
Only the tens digit changes.
lessons.try: Take away rods to subtract tens.

learn: 76 − 30: count back 3 tens: 66, 56, 46.
The ones digit stays the same.
Move up a hundred chart to subtract tens.
lessons.try: Subtract 20 and 40 from five numbers.

learn: To find 62 − 47, count up from 47 to 62.
Counting up finds the difference.
lessons.try: Use an open number line to count up.

learn: Subtract tens first, then ones.
Keep the first number whole and break the second.
lessons.try: Solve 86 − 43 and 69 − 25.

learn: Sometimes you need more ones: 52 − 17.
Trade one ten for ten ones: 52 becomes 4 tens and 12 ones.
12 − 7 = 5, 4 tens − 1 ten = 3 tens. Answer 35.
lessons.try: Use blocks to solve 43 − 18.

learn: Line up the columns. Start with the ones.
If the top ones digit is smaller, regroup a ten.
Cross out, write the new digits, then subtract.
check: Which column do you subtract first?
lessons.try: Solve 64 − 28 in columns.

learn: Make the number you subtract friendly: 63 − 29 = 63 − 30 + 1 = 34.
You took one too many, so add it back.
Great for numbers ending in 9.
lessons.try: Solve 72 − 19 and 85 − 39.

learn: Check subtraction by adding.
Addition and subtraction undo each other.
lessons.try: Check five subtraction answers with addition.

learn: Difference means how many more or fewer.
"Tom has 52 cards. Sam has 35. How many more does Tom have?" 52 − 35 = 17.
Compare problems use subtraction.
check: Difference means how many more or...
Lia read 40 pages, Ben read 26. How many more did Lia read?
lessons.try: Compare two class tallies.

learn: Some problems need two steps.
"There were 50 buns. 18 were sold, then 12 more. How many left?" 50 − 18 = 32, 32 − 12 = 20.
Solve one step at a time.
lessons.try: Solve two two-step problems with drawings.

learn: Use friendly numbers in your head.
Practise mental tricks every day.
lessons.try: Solve five subtractions without paper.

learn: Count up, break apart, regroup or compensate.
Always check with addition.
Read word problems carefully.
lessons.try: Subtraction relay with your team.

learn: Adding hundreds is like adding ones: 300 + 400 = 700.
253 + 400: only the hundreds change. 653.
10 more or 100 more: 10 more than 482 is 492. 100 more is 582.
lessons.try: Find 10 more, 10 less, 100 more and 100 less than 365.

learn: Add ones, then tens, then hundreds, regrouping when needed.
Line up the digits by place value.
check: How should you line up digits?

learn: Subtract ones, then tens, then hundreds, regrouping when needed.
542 - 187: 2 - 7 needs a ten: 12 - 7 = 5. 3 - 8 needs a hundred: 13 - 8 = 5. 4 - 1 = 3. Answer: 355.
Check by adding the answer to the number you subtracted.
lessons.try: Subtract 600 - 245.

learn: 345 + 200: only the hundreds change. 545.
Count on by hundreds.
Tens and ones stay the same.
lessons.try: Add 300 to five numbers.

learn: Add hundreds, then tens.
Mental adding saves time.
lessons.try: Solve five sums in your head.

learn: Line up hundreds, tens and ones.
Add ones, then tens, then hundreds.
lessons.try: Solve three column additions.

learn: 268 + 125: 8 + 5 = 13. Write 3, carry 1 ten.
6 + 2 + 1 = 9 tens. 2 + 1 = 3 hundreds. Answer 393.
Always add the carried number.
472 + 153: 2 + 3 = 5. 7 + 5 = 12 tens. Write 2, carry 1 hundred.
4 + 1 + 1 = 6 hundreds. Answer 625.
Ten tens make one hundred.
Line up the places and subtract ones, tens, hundreds.
Check by adding.
lessons.try: Solve three column subtractions.

learn: 452 − 128: 2 is less than 8, so trade a ten. 12 − 8 = 4.
4 tens − 2 tens = 2 tens. 4 − 1 = 3 hundreds. Answer 324.
Cross out and rewrite as you trade.
400 − 135 is tricky. Trade 1 hundred for 10 tens, then 1 ten for 10 ones.
400 becomes 3 hundreds, 9 tens and 10 ones.
lessons.try: Solve 300 − 128 with blocks.

learn: Round to the nearest hundred to estimate.
Compare your answer to the estimate.
lessons.try: Estimate, then add three pairs.

learn: "A farm has 245 sheep and 168 goats. How many animals?" 245 + 168 = 413.
"A shop had 500 pencils and sold 236." 500 − 236 = 264.
Decide add or subtract, then solve.
lessons.try: Write and solve a big-number story.

learn: Mental maths for easy numbers: 300 + 400.
Columns for harder ones: 467 + 285.
Pick what is fastest and safest.
lessons.try: Sort ten problems into mental or columns.

learn: Line up places, regroup when needed, and check.
Estimate to catch mistakes.
Practise little and often.
lessons.try: Solve a page of mixed problems.

learn: An inch is about the length of a paper clip. A foot is 12 inches, like a ruler.
Use inches for small things, like a pencil. Use feet for bigger things, like a door.
Line up the end of the object with the 0 mark on the ruler.
check: How many inches in a foot?
Which unit is best for a door?
lessons.try: Measure a pencil in inches and a table in feet.

learn: A centimetre is about the width of your fingertip. A metre is 100 centimetres.
Most countries use centimetres and metres.
The same object has more centimetres than inches because centimetres are smaller.
check: How many centimetres in a metre?
A centimetre is about the width of...
lessons.try: Measure your hand in centimetres.

learn: To estimate means to make a smart guess.
Then measure to check your estimate.
To compare, find the difference: a 9-inch book and a 6-inch book differ by 3 inches.
check: A 9-inch book and a 6-inch book differ by...
lessons.try: Estimate the length of a spoon, then measure it.

learn: We measure to know how long, tall or wide something is.
Builders, tailors and cooks all measure.
Everyone using the same units makes measuring fair.
check: Using the same units makes measuring...
lessons.try: List three jobs that need measuring.

learn: A ruler is usually 12 inches long, which is 1 foot.
A yardstick is 3 feet, or 36 inches.
Start measuring at the zero line, not the edge.
lessons.try: Measure your desk with a ruler and a yardstick.

learn: An inch is about the width of a big paper clip... or the top part of your thumb.
Small things like crayons are measured in inches.
Write in. for inches.
check: An inch is about as long as...
The short way to write inches is...
lessons.try: Measure five small things in inches.

learn: 12 inches = 1 foot. 3 feet = 1 yard.
A door is about 7 feet tall. A football field is 100 yards.
Use bigger units for bigger things.
lessons.try: Measure the classroom in feet.

learn: A centimetre is about the width of your little fingernail.
100 centimetres make 1 metre.
Write cm for centimetres.
check: A centimetre is about as wide as...
The short way to write centimetres is...
lessons.try: Measure your pencil in centimetres.

learn: A metre is about one big step, or the width of a doorway.
Use metres for rooms, hallways and playgrounds.
Write m for metres.
check: A metre is about one big...
lessons.try: Measure the hallway with a metre stick.

learn: Use small units for small things and big units for big things.
A pencil: inches or centimetres. A playground: feet, yards or metres.
The wrong unit gives silly numbers.
lessons.try: Sort objects by the best unit.

learn: Measure the same thing in inches and centimetres.
A book might be 10 inches and 25 centimetres.
Smaller units give bigger numbers.
check: The same book measured in cm shows a ___ number than in inches.
lessons.try: Measure three things in both units.

learn: An estimate is a smart guess before measuring.
Use benchmarks: your thumb is about 1 inch, your step about 1 metre.
Check your estimate by measuring.
lessons.try: Estimate and measure five things.

learn: Compare two lengths by subtracting.
A 15 cm pencil and a 9 cm crayon: 15 − 9 = 6 cm longer.
Always label the unit.
check: To find how much longer, you...
lessons.try: Compare the length of two shoes.

learn: "A ribbon is 24 inches. Mia cuts 9 inches off. How long now?" 24 − 9 = 15 inches.
"Two boards are 30 cm and 45 cm. Total?" 75 cm.
Draw a picture to help.
lessons.try: Solve three length stories.

learn: A line plot shows measurements with Xs above a number line.
Measure everyone's hand span and plot it.
The tallest stack shows the most common length.
check: A line plot uses ___ above a number line.
The tallest stack shows the most ___ length.
lessons.try: Make a line plot of pencil lengths in your group.

learn: The minute hand moves around the clock in 60 minutes.
Each number on the clock stands for 5 minutes: the 1 means 5, the 2 means 10, the 3 means 15.
When the hour hand is past 3 and the minute hand is on the 4, it is 3:20.
check: How many minutes in an hour?
When the minute hand points to 3, it is...
Hour hand past 3, minute hand on 4 is...
lessons.try: Read a clock at home at three different times.

learn: A.M. means the hours from midnight to noon. Morning.
P.M. means the hours from noon to midnight. Afternoon and evening.
You eat breakfast at 7:00 a.m. and dinner at 6:00 p.m.
lessons.try: Write three things you do and their times with a.m. or p.m.

learn: Penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢, dollar $1 = 100¢.
Count the biggest coins first: 2 quarters, 1 dime, 3 pennies = 25 + 25 + 10 + 3 = 63¢.
Use the cents sign ¢ or the dollar sign: $0.63.
check: How many cents in a dollar?
Which coins should you count first?
lessons.try: Count the coins in a pocket or jar.

learn: A clock has an hour hand (short) and a minute hand (long).
The numbers go from 1 to 12.
The hands move around the clock clockwise.
lessons.try: Make a paper clock with moving hands.

learn: When the minute hand points at 12, it's o'clock: 3:00.
When it points at 6, it's half past: 3:30.
Half an hour is 30 minutes.
lessons.try: Show 4:00 and 4:30 on your clock.

learn: Each number on the clock is 5 minutes for the minute hand.
At 1 it's 5 minutes, at 2 it's 10, at 3 it's 15.
Count by fives to read the minutes.
lessons.try: Count by fives around the clock.

learn: Read the hour hand first, then count the minutes.
Hour hand just past 2 and minute hand on 7: 2:35.
Write the time with a colon.
lessons.try: Read ten clocks to five minutes.

learn: Quarter past means 15 minutes after: 6:15.
Quarter to means 15 minutes before the hour: 6:45 is quarter to 7.
A quarter hour is 15 minutes.
lessons.try: Show quarter past and quarter to on your clock.

learn: A digital clock shows the time in numbers: 9:20.
Hours come before the colon, minutes after.
Match analog and digital times.
check: A digital clock shows time with...
lessons.try: Match five clock faces to digital times.

learn: AM is from midnight to noon. PM is from noon to midnight.
School starts in the AM. Dinner is in the PM.
Noon is 12:00 PM.
lessons.try: Make a day timeline with AM and PM events.

learn: Penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢.
A dime is smaller than a nickel but worth more.
Learn coins by look and value.
lessons.try: Sort a pile of coins by value.

learn: Start with the biggest coins and count on.
2 quarters, 1 dime, 3 pennies: 25, 50, 60, 61, 62, 63¢.
Skip count by coin value.
lessons.try: Count three handfuls of coins.

learn: 100 cents = 1 dollar. Write $1.00.
4 quarters make a dollar. 10 dimes make a dollar.
Use $ for dollars and ¢ for cents.
check: How many quarters make a dollar?
How many dimes make a dollar?
lessons.try: Make a dollar three different ways.

learn: If a toy costs 65¢ and you pay $1.00, count up to find change.
65 to 75 is 10, 75 to 100 is 25. Change is 35¢.
Always check your change.
lessons.try: Play shop with price tags and coins.

learn: "School starts at 8:00. It takes 15 minutes to walk. When should I leave?" 7:45.
"I have 3 quarters. A drink is 60¢. Can I buy it?" Yes, 75¢ > 60¢.
Read carefully and draw clocks or coins.
check: Leave at ___ to walk 15 minutes and arrive at 8:00.
lessons.try: Solve three time and money stories.

learn: A bar graph uses bars to show data. A picture graph uses symbols.
Read the scale: in some picture graphs, one symbol might stand for 2.
You can answer questions like: how many more chose apples than bananas?
check: If one symbol stands for 2, how many do 4 symbols show?
Apples 9, bananas 5: how many more chose apples?
lessons.try: Survey 10 people about their favourite colour and make a bar graph.

learn: A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides.
Triangle 3 sides, quadrilateral 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6.
A cube has 6 square faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.
check: How many sides does a pentagon have?
A shape with 4 sides is a...
How many faces does a cube have?
lessons.try: Draw a pentagon and a hexagon.

learn: Shapes can be split into equal shares.
Two equal parts are halves. Three are thirds. Four are fourths.
Equal shares of the same shape don't have to look the same shape, just the same size.
check: Which is bigger: one half or one fourth of the same pizza?
Equal shares must be the same...
lessons.try: Fold paper into thirds and colour one third.

learn: Data is information we collect, like favourite fruits.
Ask a question and tally the answers.
Tally marks are grouped in fives.
lessons.try: Survey your class on favourite pets.

learn: A picture graph uses pictures to show data.
A key tells what each picture stands for.
One smiley might stand for 2 people.
check: The ___ tells what each picture means.
lessons.try: Make a picture graph of your survey.

learn: A bar graph uses bars to show amounts.
Read the scale on the side.
Longer bars mean more.
check: A bar graph shows amounts with...
The numbers on the side are the...
lessons.try: Turn your picture graph into a bar graph.

learn: Graphs answer questions: Which is most? How many more?
Compare bars by subtracting.
Read carefully and check the scale.
check: Cats 8, dogs 5. How many more cats?
lessons.try: Write three questions about a bar graph.

learn: A polygon is a closed flat shape with straight sides.
Triangle 3 sides, quadrilateral 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6.
A circle is not a polygon.
lessons.try: Draw and name four polygons.

learn: A vertex is a corner where sides meet.
An angle is the space between two sides at a vertex.
A triangle has 3 angles and 3 vertices.
lessons.try: Count vertices on five shapes.

learn: Quadrilaterals have 4 sides and 4 angles.
Squares, rectangles, rhombuses and trapezoids are quadrilaterals.
A square has 4 equal sides and 4 square corners.
lessons.try: Sort quadrilateral cards.

learn: Solid shapes are 3D: cube, sphere, cone, cylinder, pyramid.
Faces are flat surfaces. Edges are where faces meet.
A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.
lessons.try: Find solid shapes in the classroom.

learn: Split a rectangle into rows and columns of equal squares.
2 rows of 3 squares = 6 squares.
This leads to area later.
lessons.try: Split a rectangle into 3 rows of 4 and count.

learn: Equal parts are the same size.
2 equal parts are halves, 3 are thirds, 4 are fourths (quarters).
A whole is all the parts together.
lessons.try: Fold paper into halves, thirds and fourths.

learn: Halves of a square can be rectangles or triangles.
They look different but are the same size.
Equal shares don't have to be the same shape.
check: Halves of a square can be...
Equal shares must be the same...
lessons.try: Cut squares into halves three different ways.

learn: Graphs show data. Shapes have sides, angles and faces.
Equal parts make halves, thirds and fourths.
Maths is all around you.
lessons.try: Make a poster showing what you learned this year in maths.
